sections.content: This section introduces the foundational concept of worship (yāga) in Pāñcarātra practice. It begins by linking the three modes of the Deity (para, vyūha, vibhava) to iconic worship and initiation (dīkṣā). The text affirms the necessity of worshipping the Deity in concrete forms (sākāra), especially for the benefit of others (parārtha). It outlines four primary 'seats' (catus-sthānārcanā) for worship: an icon (mūrtau), fire (agnau), a maṇḍala, or water (jalāśaye). An alternative list of four seats is also provided: one's own heart (sva-hṛt-padme), a sacred water-pot (kalaśe), the sun (sūrye), and an icon. The choice of seat depends on the devotee's spiritual and intellectual level. Worship in the heart requires advanced spiritual development, while iconic worship is presented as the easiest and safest method for all. The text quotes a verse from Viṣṇu-tattva-saṃhitā and another long verse asserting that worship (arcanā), contemplation (dhyāna), and praise (stotra) are only possible for a Godhead with form (sākāra), making iconic worship essential. The section then defines 'yāga' in the Āgama context as worship in any of the four seats and introduces its two broad varieties: bahir-yāga (external worship) and antar-yāga (internal worship). Bahir-yāga involves material objects and physical, verbal, and mental actions, aimed at eradicating defects from rajas and tamas. Iconic worship in temples or homes falls into this category. It is described as Kriyā-yoga, a path of action that leads to salvation, not bondage.
sections.summary: This section defines yāga (worship) in Pāñcarātra, emphasizing the importance of concrete, iconic forms of the Deity. It lists various 'seats' of worship, arguing that iconic worship is the most accessible. It then differentiates between external worship (bahir-yāga), which uses physical rituals and objects, and internal worship (antar-yāga).
key_concepts: Modes of the Deity (para, vyūha, vibhava)

sections.content: This section focuses on antar-yāga (internal worship), which is distinguished by its inward orientation, dispensing with concrete icons. The Deity is approached solely through mantras. This practice is performed within one's own body-mind complex, viewed as the Deity's shrine. Key procedures include nyāsa (placements), projecting the body as a temple, and identifying oneself with the Deity being worshipped. The text quotes verses from Sāttvata-saṃhitā and Jayākhya-saṃhitā to illustrate this concept of identifying with the divine ('I am that Lord Viṣṇu...'). A crucial point is made that the various divine forms (vyūha, vyūhāntara, vibhava) each have a specific mantra. The devotee must simultaneously recite the mantra and visualize the corresponding iconic form. This combined act of recitation and contemplation is what the term 'yāga' signifies in the pañca-kāla ideology. The section then provides the specific mantras and seed-syllables for the four vyūha forms (Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) from the Sāttvata-saṃhitā. It also details the nyāsa (placement) of these four forms onto the devotee's own body, from feet to head. Following this, it lists the seed-mantras for the twelve vyūhāntara-forms from Pārameśvara-saṃhitā and the thirty-eight mantras for the vibhava forms. A commentary on Sāttvata-saṃhitā is cited, explaining the origin of the seed-syllable for Padma-nābha, the first vibhava form.
sections.summary: This part details antar-yāga (internal worship), where mantras replace physical icons. It describes practices like nyāsa (placing mantras on the body) and self-identification with the Deity. It provides extensive lists of specific mantras and seed-syllables for the vyūha, vyūhāntara, and vibhava forms, emphasizing the synthesis of recitation and visualization.

sections.content: This section shifts focus to the philosophical framework underlying initiation (dīkṣā). It introduces the concept of the 'six planes or paths' (adhva-ṣaṭka), a concept shared with Śaiva-āgama. These planes are described as transformations of Lakṣmī, the energy of Para-Vāsudeva. To rise from the lowest plane (the ordinary world) and attain salvation, initiation is indispensable. The six planes are listed as: (1) Varṇādhvā (letters of the alphabet, śabda-brahma), (2) Kalādhvā (the six divine attributes), (3) Tattvādhvā (categories, i.e., the divine forms like Vāsudeva), (4) Māntrikādhvā (mantras), (5) Pādikādhvā (states of human experience like waking, dream, sleep), and (6) Bhuvanādhvā (the fourteen worlds of worldly existence). The text explains the role of each plane in the cosmic evolution and the spiritual journey. The last two planes (Pāda and Bhuvana) are considered impure (aśuddha) and must be rejected, while the first four lead to salvation. Initiation's role is to strengthen the aversion to the lower planes and facilitate ascent through the higher ones, culminating in the realization of the supreme state of Viṣṇu. The text then outlines three varieties of initiation based on the seeker's goal: (1) Para-dīkṣā for salvation (kaivalya), (2) Vyūha-dīkṣā for both worldly welfare and salvation (bhoga-kaivalya), and (3) Vaibhava-dīkṣā for worldly welfare only (bhoga). The Sāttvata-saṃhitā is cited to suggest that all three initiations are beneficial for those seeking both prosperity and emancipation.
sections.summary: This section explains the necessity of dīkṣā (initiation) for spiritual progress, framed by the concept of the 'six planes' (adhva-ṣaṭka). It details these six planes—from the material world to the realm of pure sound—and classifies them as those to be rejected and those to be pursued. It also introduces three types of initiation (Para, Vyūha, Vaibhava) corresponding to different spiritual goals (salvation, welfare, or both).

sections.content: This final section discusses the practicalities and different classifications of initiation. It emphasizes the inclusivity of Pāñcarātra, stating that everyone—devotees, advanced souls, old people, women, children, and the ignorant—is eligible. Three procedures for initiation are suggested based on wealth: an elaborate and expensive mahā-maṇḍala-yāga for the wealthy, a simple fire-ritual for the less wealthy, and initiation by a mere word of mouth for the poor. All methods are considered of equal merit. The initial initiation is into a vibhava-form mantra. Higher initiations use vyūha-forms, and the final one uses the transcendental (para) form. The text details the five consecrations (pañca-saṃskāra) involved in initiatory rites: (1) tāpa (branding with heated metallic emblems of Viṣṇu's discus and conch), (2) puṇḍra (wearing sectarian marks on the forehead), (3) nāma (bestowal of a name of Viṣṇu), (4) mantra (communication of a mantra), and (5) yāga (fire-rituals). The branding ceremony (tāpa) is highlighted as being of great importance. The section concludes by noting that later Pāñcarātra texts like Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā offer different explanations of the six planes and classify initiation differently—into gross (sthūla), subtle (sūkṣma), and transcendental (parā), relating them to different grades of priests (samayi, putraka, sādhaka, ācārya) and castes (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, etc.).
sections.summary: This section covers the practical aspects of dīkṣā, stressing its universal eligibility regardless of social status, gender, or age. It describes the five core initiatory rites (pañca-saṃskāra), with a focus on the branding ceremony (tāpa). It also notes that later texts present alternative schemas for the six planes and different classifications of initiation based on priestly grades and caste.
key_concepts: Samayi, Putraka, Sādhaka, Ācārya (Grades of priests)

chapter_summary: Chapter VI, 'PĀÑCARĀTRA PRACTICE,' provides a detailed overview of the theory and practice of worship (yāga) and initiation (dīkṣā) within the Pāñcarātra Āgamic tradition. It begins by establishing the centrality of worshipping the Deity in concrete, iconic forms (sākāra), deeming it the most accessible path for all devotees. The chapter distinguishes between two primary modes of worship: bahir-yāga, or external worship involving rituals and physical objects, and antar-yāga, or internal worship performed mentally through mantras, visualization, and identification with the Deity. A significant portion is dedicated to listing the specific mantras and seed-syllables for the vyūha, vyūhāntara, and vibhava forms of Viṣṇu, emphasizing the unity of mantra recitation and contemplation of the divine form. The chapter then elucidates the philosophical foundation for spiritual progression through the 'six planes' (adhva-ṣaṭka), a hierarchical system through which a practitioner ascends via initiation. Finally, it details the practical aspects of dīkṣā, including its universal eligibility, its different types corresponding to the seeker's goals, the five core consecratory rites (pañca-saṃskāra), and variations in classification found across different Pāñcarātra texts.
key_arguments: Worship of a deity with form (sākāra) is more practical and relevant for most practitioners than worship of a formless (nirākāra) Godhead.
Iconic worship is the easiest and safest method of worship suitable for everyone, regardless of their spiritual advancement.
Pāñcarātra practice involves two complementary forms of worship: external (bahir-yāga) for purification and internal (antar-yāga) for deep spiritual identification.
Initiation (dīkṣā) is indispensable for spiritual progress, as it is the means to transcend the lower planes of worldly existence and ascend to the divine.
The five consecrations (pañca-saṃskāra), particularly the ritual branding (tāpa), are essential rites that formally induct a devotee into the Vaiṣṇava path.
Eligibility for initiation in Pāñcarātra is universal, open to all regardless of age, gender, or social standing, reflecting an inclusive spiritual approach.
key_takeaways: Worship (yāga) can be external (with icons, fire, etc.) or internal (with mantras in the heart).
Internal worship (antar-yāga) involves visualizing the deity's form while chanting its specific mantra, and identifying one's own body with the deity's temple.
Spiritual progress is viewed as a journey through six planes of existence (adhva-ṣaṭka), from the material world to the divine source.
Initiation (dīkṣā) is the formal process that enables this journey and is categorized based on whether the goal is worldly welfare, salvation, or both.
The five key rites of initiation are tāpa (branding), puṇḍra (marks), nāma (name), mantra (sacred formula), and yāga (fire ritual).

quotations.quote:
स्थण्डिलेऽग्नौ च सूर्ये हृदयपंकजे ।
मण्डले प्रतिमायां च ततश्चित्रपटे तथा ॥
आलये च तथाकाशे स्थानेष्वाराध्यते हरिः।
निराकारे तु देवेश नार्चनं संभवेन्नृणाम् ॥
न च ध्यानं न च स्तोत्रं तस्मात्साकारमर्चयेत्।
साकारे तु कृता पूजा स्मृतिर्वा ध्यानमेव वा ।
विधिना शास्त्रदृष्टेन देव एव कृता भवेत्॥
quotations.context: Quoted to emphasize the necessity of worshipping a Godhead with form (sākāra), as worship, contemplation, and praise are considered impossible for a formless (nirākāra) deity.
Used to support the idea that the path of actions (Kriyā-yoga) in Pāñcarātra leads to salvation (naiṣkarmya), not bondage.

quotations.quote:
चतुश्चक्रे नवद्वारे देहे देवगृहे पुरा ।
न्यस्यैवमभिमानं तु मन्त्राख्यमवलम्ब्य च ॥
quotations.context: Describes the practice of antar-yāga, where one places mantras (nyāsa) on one's own body, viewing it as the 'house of God' (devagṛha).

quotations.quote: (Comm. आधार निभिहत्कण्ठचतुश्चक्रविशिष्टे नवद्वारान्विते स्वशरीरे न्यायेन भगवन्मन्दिरबुद्या मन्त्रान् विन्यस्य 'नादेवो देवनर्चये 'दिति स्वास्मिन् देवत्वाभिमानावलम्बनं कुर्यात्॥)
quotations.context: Explains the verse above, stating that one should place mantras on one's own body with the understanding that it is the Lord's temple, and cultivate the feeling of one's own divinity, based on the principle 'one who is not a god cannot worship a god'.

quotations.quote:
अहं स भगवान् विष्णुरहं नारायणे हरिः।
वासुदेवोऽह्यहं व्यापी भूतावासो निरञ्जनः।
एवं रूपमहंकारमासाद्य सृदृढं मुने ॥
quotations.context: Illustrates the process of identifying oneself with the Deity in antar-yāga: 'I am that Lord Viṣṇu, I am Nārāyaṇa Hari...'

quotations.quote:
जितं ते पुण्डरीकाक्ष वासुदेवामिद्युते ।
रागदोषादिनिर्मुक्तो समस्तगुणमूर्तिमान्।।
(ओं नमें भगवते वासुदेवाय )
quotations.context: The mantra for the vyūha form of Vāsudeva.

quotations.quote:
नाथ ज्ञानबलोत्कृष्ट नमस्ते विश्वभावन।
संकर्षण विशालाक्ष सर्वज्ञ परमेश्वर ॥
(ओं नमो भगवते संकर्षणाय ।)
quotations.context: The mantra for the vyūha form of Saṃkarṣaṇa.

quotations.quote:
देवैश्वर्यवीर्यात्मन् प्रद्युम्न जगतां पते ।
नमस्तेऽस्तु हृषीकेश सर्वेश्वर जगन्मय ।।
ओं नमो भगवते प्रद्युन्माय।)
quotations.context: The mantra for the vyūha form of Pradyumna.

quotations.quote:
स्थित्युत्पत्तिलयत्राणहेतवे शक्तितेजसे ।
जयानिरुद्ध भगवन् महापुरुष पूर्वज ॥
(ओं नमो भगवतेऽनिरुद्धाय ।)
quotations.context: The mantra for the vyūha form of Aniruddha.

quotations.quote:
आपादाज्ञ्जानुपर्यन्तमनिरुद्धं च विन्यसेत्।
नाभ्यन्तं जानुमण्डलात् प्रद्युम्नाख्यं न्यसेन्मन्त्रम्।।
नाभेराकर्णदेशं तु मन्त्रं साङ्कर्षणं न्यसेत् ।
आकर्णाद् ब्रह्मरन्ध्रान्तं चतुर्थं विनिवेद्य च।
ततस्त्वभिमतेनैव त्वास्ते पद्मासनादिना ।
स्वात्मना चातुरात्मायभिमानं समाश्रयेत्।
quotations.context: Describes the nyāsa (placement) of the four vyūha forms on the body, from feet to head.

quotations.quote:
महामण्डलयागेन हवनाद्वाथ केवलात् ।
वाचा केवलया वापि दीक्षैषा दीक्षैषा त्रिविधा पुनः ।
वित्ताद्यस्याल्पवित्तस्य द्रव्यहीनस्य च क्रमात् ॥
quotations.context: Explains the three methods of initiation based on wealth: via a grand maṇḍala-yāga, a fire ritual, or simply by word of mouth.

quotations.quote:
एवं संशुद्धदोषाणां बहुजन्मार्जितस्य च ।
कल्मषस्य विघातार्थं नरसिंहीं महामते।
कृत्वा वै साम्प्रतं दीक्षां दद्याद्वै मन्त्रपूर्वकम्।।
quotations.context: States that initiation with a mantra should be given to destroy the accumulated sins of many births.

quotations.quote: तापः पुण्ड्रस्तथा नाम मन्त्रो यागश्च पञ्चमः।
quotations.context: Lists the five consecrations (pañca-saṃskāra): tāpa, puṇḍra, nāma, mantra, and yāga.
Emphasizes the importance of being branded with the discus (cakra) to be able to take refuge in Vāsudeva.

quotations.quote:
ईक्षते कर्मण येन तद्विष्णोः परमं पदम्।
द्यति संसारमखिलं तेन दीक्षेति भण्यते ॥
quotations.context: Provides an etymological definition of dīkṣā: 'that by which one perceives the supreme state of Viṣṇu and which destroys the entire transmigratory world'.

tables_and_charts.description: A list of the twelve vyūhāntara-forms, organized into four groups of three.
tables_and_charts.data_summary: Lists the 12 forms: Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava (Group I); Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana (Group II); Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara (Group III); Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara (Group IV).

tables_and_charts.description: A list of the specific seed-mantras for the twelve vyūhāntara-forms, corresponding to the previous list.
tables_and_charts.data_summary: Provides the bīja-mantras: 1. Keśava ह्यूं, 2. Nārāyaṇa हूं, 3. Mādhava हॄं, 4. Govinda स्यूं, 5. Viṣṇu स्लूं, 6. Madhusūdana स्तूं, 7. Trivikrama क्यूं, 8. Vāmana क्लू, 9. Śrīdhara कूं, 10. Hṛṣīkeśa क्ष्यूं, 11. Padmanabha क्ष्लूं, 12. Dāmodara क्षं.

tables_and_charts.description: A numbered list of the thirty-eight mantras for the vibhava forms.
tables_and_charts.data_summary: Presents 38 mantras in the form 'ॐ [syllable] नमः।', starting with (1) ॐ नों नमः। and ending with (38) ॐ षं नमः।.

(Comm. on Sāttvata-samhitā 9,66 page 183-184). Here the seed- syllable of Viśākha-yūpa, which is the basic form of all vyūha, vyūhāntara and vibhava forms is given as न and with visarga it becomes the seed-syllable of Padma-nābha, the first of the vibhava forms.

controversial_points: The Pāñcarātra practice of universal eligibility for initiation, including for women and all castes, was a significant departure from and potentially controversial to the more restrictive, orthodox Vedic traditions of its time.
The ritual of tāpa (branding) has been a subject of debate and differing opinions among various Vaiṣṇava sects over the centuries.
alternative_viewpoints: The chapter presents two different lists for the four 'seats' of worship, indicating variance within the tradition (Page 1).

The chapter contrasts the Pāñcarātra view of the six planes (adhva-ṣaṭka) as described in Lakṣmī-tantra and Sāttvata-saṃhitā (Page 7-9) with a different order and context provided by a later text, the Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā (Page 13). This highlights the evolution and diversity of thought within Pāñcarātra itself.
The text explicitly mentions that its explanation of the six planes is a concept also familiar to Śaiva-āgama, acknowledging a parallel tradition (Page 7).
